body: The heater clicked off a while ago and the room is going cold at the edges. Twenty to five in the morning; there are four other beds in it, and the man in the fifth is lying still. There is a strip of corridor light under the door. He has one earphone in and the wire tucked inside his collar, and he is praying — not silently, but at the volume of a man counting under his breath. The words are not English. They are the words his grandmother used over him when he was small, and in the eleven months he has lived in this building he has not once said them out loud.

That is not a story about persecution, and it would cheapen it to make it one. It is a story about volume. For an enormous number of believers the daily questions of faith are not doctrinal at all. They are questions about how loud, who is on the stairs, and whether the door is properly shut.

A great many of the world’s Christians practise under some degree of legal or social pressure. It runs from paperwork and quiet trouble at work through to statutes that put conversion in front of a court, and it varies so much from street to street that generalising is usually wrong. What does not vary is the shape of it: exposure, and how much a person can afford this week.

The word in the title worth taking literally is language. We treat languages as containers — the same water, different jugs — as though anything said in one can be said in another with nothing lost but flavour. They do not behave like that. A language arrives carrying the household it was learnt in. It has the words a person was scolded in, and thanked in, and sung to sleep in, and whatever it already had for God before anybody came to explain God to it. Praying in a second language is a performance, however fluent: a person composes, checks, and hears himself. Praying in the first one is not a performance at all. It is speech, and it goes to a much older part of a person than argument ever reaches.

This band carries 40 international stations across 29 languages, and each one is hosted in its own language rather than translated into it afterwards. They sit together in one stretch of the dial, HM 320 to HM 340, which the band calls The Nations.

Doing it that way costs considerably more than the alternative, and the alternative is well understood. You make one programme properly, in one language, and have it read out in the others. It is cheap, it scales, and it sounds fine. What it cannot do is sound like somebody’s mother. A station hosted in its own language needs a person who already prays in it, who knows which phrases are worn smooth and which ones land like a slap, and who does not have to be told what the songs mean. That person is much harder to find than a translator, and there is no way to fake them.

Almost all the material a person can reach in this situation was made somewhere comfortable. It assumes a listener who can gather freely, wear the thing publicly, and treat faith as a preference rather than as an exposure. Its calls to boldness are written by people for whom boldness costs a conversation. That is provincialism rather than hypocrisy, and it would be unremarkable but for one thing. A great deal of the New Testament was written to people for whom this was the ordinary condition, and it shows in what the text bothers to say.

Read the letters with that in mind and the emphases stop looking odd. Endurance, at length. Households, constantly. What to do about work, about neighbours, about people who are watching. Very small gatherings treated as entirely sufficient, and almost nothing about buildings. The documents were written for the exact circumstances a great many of their readers are still in, and it is the comfortable reader who has to work to make them fit.
Which is why the delivery matters as much as the content here, and why it is worth being precise about what a frequency actually is.

Consider what worship has usually needed in order to exist. A building, or a room somebody lends. A book, which has to live on a shelf where it can be seen. A gathering, which is a diary entry and a set of faces. A recording, which is a file somebody owns and a shelf again. Every one of those is a possession, and a possession sits somewhere and can be found. A frequency is none of that. It is a number a person keeps in their head and a sound that exists only while it is sounding. This is not a claim about safety, and nobody should dress it up as one. It is a claim about weight.
A frequency weighs nothing, and it leaves nothing on a shelf.

A man in his sixties parks outside his own house on a Tuesday evening and does not get out. He switches the engine off and the bonnet ticks as it cools. Through the front window he can see the television going and the back of his son-in-law’s head, and he knows exactly how the next four hours will run. He has perhaps fifteen minutes before anybody wonders where he has got to. He puts a station on through the car speakers, low, just above the rain on the roof, and it is in his own language, and a man he will never meet is praying in it about work, and a daughter, and being tired. He does not join in. He sits with both hands on the wheel until the song after it has finished, and then goes in and eats his dinner.

Nothing in that required a building, a register, a decision or a conversation. It required a language and fifteen minutes in a parked car. That is the mechanism, and it is a great deal smaller than most of what the church builds.

It is also, plainly, not a church, and it must never be sold as one. A frequency cannot baptise anybody. It cannot sit up with a family, or know a name, or notice that somebody has stopped coming. It cannot break bread, and it cannot be corrected by the people it teaches, which is a serious lack. Anyone who tells a person under pressure that a stream is a substitute for a body of believers is selling them a comfort that will not hold weight.

But the gaps between gatherings are the actual problem, and for some listeners those gaps are measured in months. A language goes quiet before it goes. The tongue a person prays in gets stiff exactly as any other tongue does, and the vocabulary that goes first is the specific one — the words for mercy, for covenant, for the particular thing being asked. What a station in that language does, running under ordinary hours, is keep those words moving. It is not the meal. It is what keeps a person hungry between meals, which is not nothing.

So the argument here is narrow. A language is not a wrapper around a faith; it is part of how the faith is held. Making worship available in a person’s own language, hosted by somebody who lives in it, is not a courtesy extended to the periphery. It is a recognition that the periphery is where most of this has always happened, and that the earliest documents of the faith were written to people in precisely that position.
All of which stays theoretical until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The Nations block runs from HM 320 to HM 340 and it is the busiest part of this dial. 46 of the band’s 121 frequencies are sounding now and a good share of them are in that stretch — HM 328.70 Inspire Crown in Arabic, HM 337.70 Vietnam Inspire, HM 336.60 Japan Inspire, HM 339.90 Pilipinas Inspire in Tagalog, and a long row of others. Higher up, from HM 340 to HM 360, sits The Upper Room, which is the prayer block. HM 356.70 Jubilee Prayers in Hindi lives there — assigned, in build, and not yet on air, so nothing plays there today.

If you want one frequency, take HM 332.10 Inspire India. It is on air, it is hosted in Hindi rather than dubbed into it, and it makes this article’s argument audible in about four minutes. Put it on and you will notice one thing before anything else: the singing does not sound like a translation of a chorus you already know. The cadences are not borrowed. Whatever your own first language happens to be, hearing worship carried properly in a language that is not a guest in its own sentence tends to reset the ear — and if Hindi is the language somebody was sung to sleep in, that is not a demonstration at all. That is home, arriving quietly through a phone at an hour when nobody is watching.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays; the whole thing is built for inexpensive handsets and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make an account while you are on it. It is free, it carries your favourites across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for — which is how the next language gets built.

Take this as an invitation rather than an offer. If you are somewhere the volume knob is not a real decision, put HM 332.10 on this week anyway and let it run while you do something else, because it is worth knowing what worship sounds like when it is not in your own idiom. And if you are somewhere it is a real decision, you understood every word of this article before you started reading it, and the only new information in it is a number. Keep the number in your head. That is where it is meant to live.
